name: History of Java
overview: Java started as Oak, a language for consumer devices. In three stops, see how it went public, made programs portable, and kept evolving.

sections.title: 1991 to 1996: Oak becomes Java
sections.content: James Gosling and Sun Microsystems' Green Team began work on Oak in 1991. Sun announced it as Java in 1995 and released JDK 1.0 in 1996.

sections.title: Why Java caught on
sections.content: Compile once, run on a compatible Java Virtual Machine (JVM). The same bytecode can run on Windows, Linux, or macOS. That is Write Once, Run Anywhere. No second compilation needed.

images.caption: One class file can run on compatible JVMs on different operating systems.

sections.title: Five releases worth remembering
sections.content: Oracle acquired Sun in 2010. These releases show how the language evolved.

subsections.title: Java 5 and 8
subsections.content: Java 5 made collections type-safe with generics. Java 8 added lambdas and streams, making it easier to express what to do with a collection.

subsections.title: Java 17, 21, and 25
subsections.content: Java 17 finalized sealed classes. Java 21 finalized virtual threads. Java 25 let beginners write a first program without spelling out the whole class.

keyPoints: For your 30-second recap, connect three things: where Oak began, why bytecode could travel, and which Java release changed how you write code.

interviewQA.question: Who created Java, and why?
interviewQA.answer: James Gosling and the Green Team at Sun Microsystems started Oak in 1991 for consumer electronics.

interviewQA.question: How does Write Once, Run Anywhere work?
interviewQA.answer: The compiler produces bytecode. Each platform provides a compatible JVM that can run it.

interviewQA.question: Which Java releases are LTS?
interviewQA.answer: Oracle designates Java 8, 11, 17, 21, and 25 as long-term support releases.
